hints: Think about where DNA polymerase has the most trouble finishing its copy - at the start in the middle, or right at the very tips of the long DNA molecule?
walkthrough:
Why the ends are at risk**
Imagine copying a long zip right to the very tip - the copying enzyme, DNA polymerase, cannot quite finish the extreme end each time. In a linear chromosome this means a little DNA could be lost from the tips at every replication.

Where the protection sits**
To stop this eating into useful genes, each end has a stretch of repeated, non-coding DNA that acts as a disposable buffer. That protective cap is at both tips, so drawing your line to either rounded end of Fig. 1.1 correctly shows its location.
Final answer: Label G with a line to either tip / end of the chromosome (telomere).

hints: Count the chromatids in Fig. 1.1 - is it an X-shape with two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, or a single rod with one centromere constriction?
walkthrough:
Reading the structure in Fig. 1.1**
You are sitting beside me looking at Fig. 1.1 together. It is a single rod with one narrow centromere region, not an X-shape. That means it is made of one DNA molecule - one chromatid only.

When chromosomes look like this**
For most of early mitosis chromosomes are X-shaped, with two sister chromatids. They only become single-chromatid rods after the sisters are pulled apart. That splitting happens in anaphase and the single chromatids remain separate in telophase.

hints: Remember that mitosis only divides the nucleus - what is the separate process called that then pinches the cytoplasm in two to make two whole cells?
walkthrough:
Two separate divisions**
Think of cell division in two jobs. First the nucleus divides so each end gets an identical set of chromosomes - that is mitosis. Then the whole cytoplasm and cell surface must split to make two separate cells.

Naming the cytoplasm split**
That second job, the physical division of cytoplasm to give two genetically identical daughter cells, has its own name. It is cytokinesis, occurring at the end of the mitotic cell cycle, after telophase.

hints: Think about how a cell detects a chemical message arriving from outside - what general job title do we give to a membrane protein that specifically binds that messenger?
walkthrough:
Detecting messages from outside**
Extracellular messengers such as growth factors cannot just diffuse through the membrane to act. They must be recognised at the surface by a protein or glycoprotein with a specific binding site, like a lock fitting one key.

The correct term**
Any protein or glycoprotein in the cell surface membrane that binds a signalling molecule and then triggers a response inside, for example to continue or stop the cell cycle, is called a receptor.
